Shares are of all n ≤ N. At every one of the ten checkpoints from N = 10⁶ to 10⁹ the share of increases lies between 39.67% and 42.13%. Since every gap after the first is even, the local rate of increases drops each time pn/n passes an even number, and the cumulative share follows slowly: as pn/n passes 18, between N = 10⁷ and 2.5·10⁷, it falls from 42.13% to 40.03%. Gallagher's model, in which gaps divided by log p are exponentially distributed, would put the limit at 1/e ≈ 36.8%, approached very slowly; that is a heuristic, not a theorem, and nothing here tests it. Three checks on the counts. The predicate reproduces all 10,000 terms of the b-file of OEIS A387591, the primes pn at which pn/n increases. Two deliberately wrong versions of it (reversed inequality, shifted index) fail that comparison. A third, ≤ for <, passes because it is equivalent: (n+1)pn = n·pn+1 would force n to divide pn, so n = pn once n ≥ 2, which never happens, and n = 1 gives 4 ≠ 3. The sieve's pN equals the known value at N = 10⁶, 10⁷, 10⁸ and 10⁹. A second implementation, written separately in numpy (a segmented sieve over odd numbers, testing the increase in the rearranged form n·(pn+1 − pn) > pn), reproduces every count at N = 10⁶, 10⁷, 10⁸ and 10⁹ exactly. At 10⁹ that is 397,737,673 increases and 386,645,693, 120,861,061, 37,365,515 and 1,032,888 gaps above 1, 2, 3 and 6 times log pn.
REPLAY: The release carries a Lean proof of both results at once, OAI.Problem344.large_gaps_and_ratio_density: its first half is Theorem 1.1 for every real C > 0, its second the positive lower density of the indices where pn/n increases. The comparator challenge, OpenAI's file stating the theorem with its proof left as sorry for a solution to match, is ComparatorChallenges/PrimeGaps.lean. The proof is 56 modules (22,533 lines; 1,118 theorems and 175 lemmas) on Lean 4.34.1 and Mathlib d13f23b7, and it imports nothing but Mathlib and its own directory. Our source audit found no axiom, sorry, admit, native_decide, set_option, macro, elab, syntax, unsafe, implemented_by, extern, opaque, partial def or #eval; there are six uses of decide. Our replay built all 56 modules with 0 errors in 11 min 40 s of wall time (06:10–06:22 UTC on 21 October), running at most four lean processes at once; no module took more than 26 s, and the largest peak in any one process was 6.8 GiB. #print axioms gives exactly propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for the theorem, for the gap theorem OAI.LargePrimeGaps.main, for siegelWalfisz and for bombieriVinogradov. The theorem's type and all six definitions it unfolds through (prime and primeAt, both pn = Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n − 1); the set of large-gap indices; the counting function; the lower density; the set of ratio increases) print identically in the challenge and in the solution under pp.all, Lean's fully explicit printing, which lets two statements be compared exactly. We mutation-tested the matcher six ways: a changed numeral in a definition, a changed inequality in the theorem, a challenge without sorryAx, a solution with an extra axiom, a missing definition (which must exit with "cannot see", not "mismatch"), and the unmodified logs. Each gave the expected verdict. A planted sorry is reported as sorryAx (the axiom Lean records for a missing proof), and the gap theorem applied at C = 0 fails to typecheck.
BRIDGE: #print axioms gives the standard three for erdos_968 and for the two lemmas it rests on. The controls: making FC's u divide by n + 2 breaks the index-shift lemma, and replacing FC's set by the decreasing one, {n | u n > u (n + 1)} (Erdős and Prachar's own theorem, which OpenAI's library does not prove), breaks the counting step. Neither compiles.
LEANLABEL: OpenAI's own Lean proves Theorem 1.1 (for every C > 0 there is c(C) > 0 such that, for every large N, at least c(C)·N of the indices n ≤ N have p_{n+1} − p_n > C·log p_n) together with Corollary 1.2 (p_n/n increases on a set of positive lower density). On the way it proves Bombieri–Vinogradov, which the paper assumes, from a proof of Siegel–Walfisz; Mathlib has neither. Kernel-replayed on our machine on 21 Oct 2026 (56 modules, 0 errors, standard axioms, statement and all six definitions matched to the comparator challenge under pp.all). A kernel-checked bridge of ours derives from it a verbatim copy of Formal Conjectures' erdos_968, whose indexing and lower density differ from OpenAI's — see our /day entry
ROUTE: The paper's one deep input is the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem, quoted in the endpoint form recorded by Bombieri, Friedlander and Iwaniec. The Lean proves that theorem too. bombieriVinogradov (Main.lean) comes from siegelWalfisz through Vaughan's identity and the multiplicative large sieve. The large sieve, the Pólya–Vinogradov inequality and Siegel's ineffective lower bound for L(1, χ) at quadratic characters (quadratic_siegel, via the classical product ζ(s)L(s,χ)L(s,ψ)L(s,χψ)) are all proved in the same directory. Mathlib at this commit has none of these theorems. Bombieri–Vinogradov (for moduli up to xθ, θ < 1/2), Siegel–Walfisz and the large sieve are not new to Lean, though: a public repository, kimihiro64/bombieri-vinogradov (release v0.1.0, 5 September 2026, three weeks before the paper's date), states a sorry-free proof of Bombieri–Vinogradov in that range, with Siegel–Walfisz and the large sieve on the way. We have not built it. Our Lean seat checked that both definitions are faithful (Bombieri–Vinogradov in its endpoint form, the one the paper cites, which is weaker than the textbook form with a maximum over y ≤ x) and are not vacuous. BombieriVinogradov says that for every A there is b with Σq ≤ x1/2(log x)−b max(c,q)=1 |ψ(x; q, c) − x/φ(q)| ≤ M·x(log x)−A for large x, the form the paper cites. SiegelWalfisz bounds |ψ(x, χ) − [χ = 1]·x| by M·x(log x)−A for every primitive χ of conductor at most (log x)B. Both include q = 1, so each contains the prime number theorem with a log-power error. The Siegel–Walfisz proof is not the textbook one. It proves no zero-free region to the left of Re s = 1. Instead, for every ε > 0 it proves lower bounds |L(σ + it, χ)| ≥ c(ε)·((q + 2)(|t| + 2))−ε for 1 ≤ σ ≤ 2, uses Siegel's bound for real characters near t = 0, and integrates a Riesz mean by parts repeatedly along Re s = 1. The route is valid, and the kernel checked every step. Otherwise the Lean follows the printed construction: τ = 1/8, λ = C + 1, r = √k with k a perfect square, the same alternating levels and the same profile from Lemma 4.1. It takes a smaller ε, λ²/(16D) with D = λ + λ²cG² + 1, uses a detector constant one larger than the paper's, and does not normalise the weight by w. The seat's table, mapping each printed statement to its declaration, is in the bundle. These differences, and the following ones, are of exposition. The Lean replaces all three of the paper's uses of the prime number theorem with Chebyshev-type bounds from Mathlib, so its corollary takes C = 2/log 2 instead of 2, and its constant is δ/(6(log 4 + 1)(C + 1)) instead of δ/(4λ). It proves the error terms of Proposition 5.1 and Lemma 5.4 only as o(1), uniformly in the shifts, not at the printed rates; nothing downstream needs the rates. And OpenAI's scope note for the formalization (docs/026.md) mentions only the corollary, though the comparator checks Theorem 1.1 as well.
LEANCHECKER: Mathlib's compiled files came from its cache, so we then ran leanchecker --fresh over the whole closure of our bridge below, which imports OpenAI's RatioCorollary and so covers all 56 of OpenAI's modules, Mathlib and the bridge. It re-checks every declaration from scratch. It exited with code 0 after 3,456 s (peak memory 8.2 GiB); a missing-module control exits 1.
WORLD: The world seat (a separately briefed AI reader with web access) read the primary sources. Novelty. The strongest earlier unconditional result we found is the one the paper cites, Theorem 5 of Bazzanella, Languasco and Zaccagnini (Trans. AMS 362, 2010): it counts primes p ≤ X with no prime in (p, p + λ log X], so it counts gaps, for every λ < 2/B with B = 3.454, that is λ < 0.579. A later sieve constant might push their argument slightly higher; we did not check. Their Theorem 3 reaches λ ≈ 1.145, improving Cheer and Goldston (1987), but counts integer starting points, which a few huge gaps can supply. Tao's 2019 MathOverflow answer (332888) gets gaps for λ < 1/4 and names the missing input. In 1965 Erdős wrote: "Unfortunately I cannot prove that the upper density of the integers n for which dn > log n is positive", and named the obstacle Tao would name sixty years later: a lower bound for the total of the large gaps says nothing "because of possible very large values of dn" ([Er65b], p. 202; we read the scan). The limit-point results (Banks–Freiberg–Maynard, Pintz, Merikoski) and the large-gap results give infinitely many n, not a positive proportion. What was asked. Erdős and Prachar's paper (Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg 25, 1961/62, p. 256) asks explicitly for lower density, for both the increases and the decreases, proves it for the decreases on the spot, and then says: "Es scheint schwierig zu sein, zu beweisen, daß die k mit pk/k < pk+1/(k+1) positive untere Dichte haben" (it seems difficult to prove that the k with pk/k < pk+1/(k+1) have positive lower density; we read the scan). So the hedge on erdosproblems.com ("most likely meant positive lower density") is settled by the primary source; [Er65b], p. 204, says only "density". What the paper leaves out. Its paragraph on conditional results cites Gallagher and Jha, but not the route through the Riemann hypothesis and pair correlation (Heath-Brown 1982, Corollary 1; Theorem 6 of Bazzanella–Languasco–Zaccagnini; Tao's comment of 10 September 2025 on the problem's thread). It also leaves out Erdős's 1965 sentence. These are omissions, not errors; the paper makes no priority claim beyond answering Erdős and Prachar. Citations. Ten were checked at the cited place, and all ten say what the paper says. They are Gallagher 1976 (Theorem 1 and p. 5, equation (3)); Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec (p. 206, (1.4), the endpoint form, with ψ defined on p. 204); Goldston–Yıldırım (p. 6, (2.14), which squares tuple approximations of different sizes); Maynard 2015 (§6, p. 404, and §7); Jha (Theorems 1.4 and 1.6, under a strong uniform Hardy–Littlewood hypothesis); Tao's MathOverflow answer; and the two Erdős–Prachar and Bazzanella–Languasco–Zaccagnini statements above. Other claims and criticism. We found none. The seat searched arXiv math.NT from January 2025 to 20 October 2026 (8,279 records) plus the 21 October listing, erdosproblems.com, Tao's blog and Mastodon, Hacker News, Bluesky, and the Formal Conjectures issues; it could not search the Lean Zulip, X or Reddit. Bloom's post of 8 October lists #968 among the claims, without endorsement, and paraphrases the theorem as gaps above C·log n. Tao's erdosproblems database still lists #968 as open (last updated 31 August 2025). Formal Conjectures marked it solved on 11 October (PR #6898, merged 08:10 UTC) on the strength of the Lean link. That PR lists the statements whose link needs a "routine transport" to match the repository's statement; #968 is not on the list, though it needs one, and our bridge supplies it.

READSUMMARY: Our main reading seat, an AI (Claude Opus 5.5), read all five sections line by line and found no gap; three further hostile AI seats, two on the mathematics and one on the sources, found none either
READING: The main seat (Claude Opus 5.5, like every seat here) read §§1–5 line by line and found no gap; its step-by-step notes are in the bundle. Three hostile AI referee seats, each told to refute the paper and to quote what it objected to, found none either, and a fourth read the Lean against the paper. They run on the same model as the main seat, so they are correlated readers, not independent ones. Seat O took §§2–4 and the corollary. It re-derived both Cauchy–Schwarz steps and the order of the quantifiers (K<sub>λ</sub> fixed before ε, the fourth-moment bound M allowed to depend on ε). It checked the prime-deletion identity (8) directly from the definition of the divisor sums, with exact divisors and Möbius values and random real test functions, at twelve events where m + a is prime. The two sides agree to 2·10⁻¹⁶; at composite m + a, the negative control, they differ by 0.05 to 0.40. It verified (4) and the signed derivative f<sub>j</sub> + Tf<sub>j+1</sub> symbolically, built an explicit smooth profile for Lemma 4.1 and checked its three identities numerically, and evaluated w and v for the family of Proposition 4.2 in two ways. At k = 4 and λ = 1, quadrature of the definitions and Monte Carlo through (10) and (11) agree: w ≈ 0.9414 and v/λ ≈ 0.7239 both ways. At large k, v/λ falls like 2/r, inside the bound (12). Two observations of its own. The deletion identity (8) uses only that m + a has no prime factor below X<sup>1/8</sup>, and the primes enter only through moduli up to X<sup>1/4</sup>, half the Bombieri–Vinogradov range. Its heuristic conclusion: a suitably rough set with prime-like local densities and that level of distribution should behave the same way, so the method should not run into the parity barrier, the classical reason sieves cannot isolate primes. We have not checked this. And the constants are enormous: at λ = 3, with β = 0.1, the profile of Lemma 4.1 needs log R ≈ 33, and the printed bounds (10) and (12) take hold only once k is of order 10¹⁴. Computed there through the characteristic function of S<sub>k</sub> (checked first against the Monte Carlo at λ = 1), the family does what the proposition says: at k = 10¹⁵, w = 1 to ten digits and v/λ = 6.3·10⁻⁸ = 2/r, inside (12) by six orders of magnitude. The proof therefore gives no usable size for c(C), and the paper claims none. Seat T took §5. The printed rate O(L<sup>−1/2</sup>(log L)<sup>A</sup>) in Proposition 5.1, uniform in the shifts, is what the printed argument proves; the Lean proves only o(1), which is all the application uses. The hypothesis B ≥ 1 is really used: the Euler-product tail beyond the largest shift difference is O(L<sup>−B</sup>), and B < 1/2 would lose the printed rate. H<sub>p</sub>(0) is the local factor of the singular series in both the marked and the unmarked case; floating-point numerics on 400 random patterns, collisions included, agree to 4·10⁻¹⁵. Bombieri–Vinogradov is used inside its range. And c<sub>G</sub> is correctly squared in C<sub>*</sub> = λ + λ²c<sub>G</sub>²: in the off-diagonal detector term both primes b ≠ c are replaced by squared detectors, which makes two fibres of size two (a fibre is a group of divisor coordinates sharing one shift), each contributing ∫G′² = c<sub>G</sub>. OpenAI's Lean has the same squared c<sub>G</sub>; its detector constant is λ + λ²c<sub>G</sub>² + 1, one larger. T's main remark: Proposition 5.1 says its constant C "depend[s] only on the functions and κ", but for fibres of size three or more, needed only for E Z⁴, the proof defines C through an arbitrary smooth extension and never argues that the choice does not matter. The choice does not in fact matter: apply (13) to one fixed admissible set of shifts. Only finiteness is used anyway. Exposition notes, none of them load-bearing. Proposition 2.1 states E W<sub>X</sub> → 1, and neither the proof nor the Lean uses it. All three uses of the prime number theorem (the corollary, the passage from X to N, and Q ≤ h<sup>1/2</sup> in Lemma 5.4) need only Chebyshev's bounds, which is what the Lean uses. The "1" in "choose λ > max{C, 1}" is never used. The letter B names at least four different things (an interval label, B<sub>R</sub> in Lemma 4.1, an endpoint of the support of g, and the shift exponent in Proposition 5.1). In two places the text rendering of the PDF looked wrong, a subset count printed as "2MR − 1" in the justification of (26) and log Δ ≤ "2s log(Kh)" in Lemma 5.4; the TeX has 2<sup>M</sup> − 1 and the binomial coefficient C(s, 2), so these are extraction artefacts, not typos.
